mbti.title: Free MBTI test: 16 personality types in 32 questions — cv.cm
mbti.description: Take a free MBTI-style personality test. Answer 32 statements and get your four-letter type (like INFJ or ESTP) with the strength of each preference. No sign-up.
mbti.lede: Find your four-letter type: where you get energy (E/I), how you take in information (S/N), how you decide (T/F), and how you organize your life (J/P).
about: The 16 types come from Carl Jung's theory of psychological types, later developed by Katharine Briggs and Isabel Myers. Each letter is one side of a pair, and the percentages show how strongly you lean that way. A result near 50% means you use both sides.
This is an independent, MBTI-style test written for cv.cm. It is not the official Myers-Briggs Type Indicator® assessment and is not affiliated with The Myers-Briggs Company.

faq.q: Is this the official MBTI test?
faq.a: No. The official MBTI® assessment is sold through certified practitioners. This free test uses the same four preference pairs with its own questions.

faq.q: What do the four letters mean?
faq.a: E or I: Extraversion or Introversion. S or N: Sensing or Intuition. T or F: Thinking or Feeling. J or P: Judging or Perceiving.

faq.q: Why did I get a different type last time?
faq.a: If one pair is close to 50%, a small change in your answers flips the letter. Look at the percentages: the strong preferences are the stable part of your type.

faq.q: Can my type change?
faq.a: Your core preferences tend to stay fairly stable in adulthood, but stress, a new job, or a new stage of life can shift how you answer.

ISTJ.name: ISTJ · The Inspector

ISTP.name: ISTP · The Craftsperson

ISFJ.name: ISFJ · The Protector

ISFP.name: ISFP · The Artist

INFP.name: INFP · The Idealist

big-five.title: Free Big Five personality test (IPIP 50 questions) — cv.cm
big-five.description: Take the free Big Five (OCEAN) personality test with the public-domain IPIP 50-item questionnaire. See your openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism scores. No sign-up.
big-five.lede: Measure the five traits psychologists use most: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism. 50 short statements, results as five scores out of 100.
about: The Big Five (also called the Five-Factor Model or OCEAN) is the best-researched model of personality. Instead of putting you in a box, it places you on five independent scales, so everyone gets a unique profile.

This test uses the 50-item Big-Five Factor Markers from the International Personality Item Pool (IPIP), developed by Lewis Goldberg and placed in the public domain. Scores here are compared to the scale range, not to a population sample, so 50 means the middle of the scale.

faq.q: What does OCEAN stand for?
faq.a: Openness to experience, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism, the five broad traits in the model.

faq.q: Is a high score better?
faq.a: No. Each end of a trait has strengths. Low extraversion goes with focus and calm; low agreeableness with candor and independence.

faq.q: Is the Big Five more scientific than MBTI?
faq.a: Most personality researchers prefer the Big Five: its traits are measured as continuous scores and predict outcomes like job performance and wellbeing in many studies.

faq.q: Where do the questions come from?
faq.a: From the IPIP 50-item Big-Five Factor Markers by Lewis Goldberg, a public-domain questionnaire used widely in research.

introvert.title: Free introvert or extrovert test (IPIP, 20 questions) — cv.cm
introvert.description: Are you an introvert, an ambivert or an extrovert? Rate 20 public-domain IPIP statements and get a score out of 80 with practical tips. Free, no sign-up.
introvert.lede: Find out where you sit between introversion and extroversion. 20 short statements from a research questionnaire, a score out of 80, and what it means for your energy, work and friendships.
about: Extraversion is one of the Big Five traits. People high in it gain energy from company, talk easily and enjoy being seen. People low in it, introverts, prefer smaller groups and quiet time, and think before they speak. Most people land somewhere in the middle: ambiverts.

The 20 statements are the extraversion scale of the 100-item Big-Five Factor Markers from the International Personality Item Pool (IPIP), developed by Lewis Goldberg and placed in the public domain. Half are reverse-scored. The cut-offs sit at 40% and 60% of the scale range (below 40% introvert, 40–60% ambivert, above 60% extrovert); they are not population norms.
Introversion is not shyness. Shyness is worry about being judged; introversion is about where your energy comes from. An introvert can be confident and socially skilled, and an extrovert can be shy.

faq.q: What is an ambivert?
faq.a: Someone in the middle of the scale: outgoing in some settings, happy alone in others. Most people are ambiverts.

faq.q: Is it better to be an extrovert?
faq.a: No. Extroverts often find networking and group work easier; introverts often do well at deep, focused work and one-to-one listening. Both can learn the skills of the other.

faq.q: Where do the questions come from?
faq.a: From the IPIP 100-item Big-Five Factor Markers by Lewis Goldberg, a public-domain item pool used widely in research. This test uses its 20 extraversion items.

faq.q: Can my result change?
faq.a: Your basic level of extraversion is fairly stable in adulthood, but it shifts a little with age, role and mood. Retake the test in a few months and compare.

enneagram.description: Free Enneagram personality test. Rate 36 statements to see which of the nine Enneagram types fits you best, with scores for all nine. No sign-up.
enneagram.lede: Discover which of the nine Enneagram types drives you: what you want most, what you fear, and how you act under stress.
about: The Enneagram describes nine personality types, each organized around a core motivation. Most people see a little of themselves in several types; your main type is the one whose motivation feels most like home.
This short test was written for cv.cm. Read the descriptions of your top two or three types and decide which fits best: self-recognition is how the Enneagram is meant to be used.

faq.q: What are the nine Enneagram types?
faq.a: 1 Reformer, 2 Helper, 3 Achiever, 4 Individualist, 5 Investigator, 6 Loyalist, 7 Enthusiast, 8 Challenger, 9 Peacemaker.

faq.q: What is a wing?
faq.a: Your wing is one of the two types next to your main type on the Enneagram circle (a 4 can have a 3 or 5 wing). Your second-highest score is a hint if it sits next to your main type.

faq.q: My top scores are close. Which is my type?
faq.a: Read each description and ask which core fear and desire feels most true over your whole life, not just lately.

faq.q: Is the Enneagram scientific?
faq.a: Research support is limited compared with the Big Five. Many people still find it a useful language for motivation and growth.

eq.title: Free emotional intelligence test (EQ test) with scores for 4 skills — cv.cm
eq.description: Free EQ test online. Rate 20 statements to score your self-awareness, self-management, empathy and relationship skills, with what each score means and how to build it. No sign-up.
eq.lede: Emotional intelligence is the skill of noticing, understanding and handling emotions, your own and other people's. Rate 20 statements and see your score in each of its four areas.
about: This test follows the four areas of Daniel Goleman's model of emotional intelligence: self-awareness (knowing what you feel and why), self-management (handling those feelings), social awareness (reading other people) and relationship management (getting along, influencing and resolving conflict).

The statements were written for cv.cm. It is a self-report check, not the licensed EQ-i or MSCEIT, and a self-report shows how you see yourself. Each area is scored from 0 to 100: below 40 is low, above 60 high. Unlike IQ, these are skills, and they improve with practice.

faq.q: What is a good EQ score?
faq.a: There is no pass mark here. A score above 60 in an area means you see that skill as a strength; below 40 marks the area most worth practising. Look at the balance between the four areas rather than one number.

faq.q: Can you improve emotional intelligence?
faq.a: Yes. Naming your feelings, pausing before you react, asking people how they see a situation and listening without planning your answer are skills that grow with practice.

faq.q: Is EQ more important than IQ?
faq.a: They measure different things. IQ tests reasoning; EQ is about handling emotions and people. Both matter, and EQ matters most in work that depends on teamwork, leadership and service.

faq.q: How accurate is a self-report EQ test?
faq.a: It shows how you see yourself, which can differ from how others see you. For a fuller picture, ask a few people who know you well to answer the questions about you.

temperament.title: Four temperaments test: sanguine, choleric, melancholic or phlegmatic? — cv.cm
temperament.description: Free four temperaments test: rate 20 statements to see whether you are mostly sanguine, choleric, melancholic or phlegmatic, with your score for each. No sign-up; answers stay in your browser.
temperament.lede: Lively, driven, thoughtful or easygoing? Rate 20 statements to find which of the four classical temperaments sounds most like you, and how much of the other three you have.
about: The four temperaments are one of the oldest personality ideas: Greek physicians linked them to the four bodily humors, and the philosopher Immanuel Kant later described them as types of feeling and acting. Sanguine people are sociable and cheerful, choleric people driven and decisive, melancholic people deep and careful, phlegmatic people calm and steady.

The humor theory is long gone, and modern psychology describes personality with traits such as the Big Five instead. The four types are still a handy, memorable way to talk about style. The statements here were written for cv.cm; most people are a mix, so look at all four scores, not just the top one.

faq.q: What are the four temperaments?
faq.a: Sanguine (outgoing, cheerful, spontaneous), choleric (ambitious, decisive, quick to anger), melancholic (thoughtful, detail-minded, sensitive) and phlegmatic (calm, patient, easygoing).

faq.q: Is the four temperaments theory scientific?
faq.a: Not in its original form: the idea that body fluids shape character was abandoned long ago. The four styles roughly line up with combinations of extraversion and emotional stability, which are well studied. Treat the result as a conversation starter.

faq.q: Can I be two temperaments?
faq.a: Yes. Most people have one or two strong temperaments and some of the others. Your result shows all four scores so you can see your blend.

faq.q: Which temperament is best?
faq.a: None. Each has strengths and blind spots: the sanguine brings energy, the choleric drive, the melancholic depth and the phlegmatic calm.

faq.q: What are the five love languages?
faq.a: Words of affirmation, quality time, receiving gifts, acts of service, and physical touch.

faq.q: Can I have more than one love language?
faq.a: Yes. Most people have one or two that matter most and others that matter a little. The chart shows all five.

faq.q: Is the love language idea backed by research?
faq.a: Studies give it mixed support: partners who show love in many ways tend to be happier overall. It works best as a conversation starter, not a rule.

faq.q: Is this the official quiz?
faq.a: No. It is an independent quiz built on the same five categories, not affiliated with Gary Chapman or his publisher.

attachment.title: Free attachment style test: secure, anxious or avoidant? — cv.cm
attachment.description: Free attachment style quiz for adults. Answer 16 statements about close relationships to see whether your style is secure, anxious, avoidant or fearful-avoidant. No sign-up.
attachment.lede: How do you act in close relationships? This quiz measures attachment anxiety and avoidance and places you in one of four styles.
about: Attachment theory began with John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth's studies of children and was extended to adult romantic relationships by Hazan and Shaver. Modern research measures two dimensions: anxiety (fear of rejection) and avoidance (discomfort with closeness).

Your style comes from where you fall on both: low on both is secure. This short quiz was written for cv.cm and is based on that two-dimension model. Styles can change with time and with supportive relationships.

faq.q: What are the four attachment styles?
faq.a: Secure (low anxiety, low avoidance), anxious (high anxiety), avoidant (high avoidance), and fearful-avoidant (high on both).

faq.q: Can my attachment style change?
faq.a: Yes. A long, stable relationship, therapy, and conscious practice can move people toward security, which researchers call earned security.

faq.q: Should I answer about my current partner?
faq.a: Answer about how you generally feel in close relationships, not only about one person.

faq.q: Which style is best?
faq.a: Secure attachment is linked with the most relationship satisfaction, but every style makes sense as a response to past experience, and each can grow.

love-style.title: Free love style test: Lee's six styles of love (Eros, Storge, Agape…) — cv.cm
love-style.description: Free love style quiz based on John Alan Lee's six styles: passionate (Eros), playful (Ludus), friendship (Storge), practical (Pragma), possessive (Mania) and selfless (Agape). Rate 24 statements, no sign-up.
love-style.h1: Love style test: how do you love?
love-style.lede: Do you fall fast and hard, or does love grow slowly from friendship? Rate 24 statements to find your main love style among the six described by sociologist John Alan Lee.
about: In 1973 the sociologist John Alan Lee described six styles of loving, named with Greek and Latin words: Eros (passionate), Ludus (playful), Storge (friendship), Pragma (practical), Mania (possessive) and Agape (selfless). Most people mix several, and the mix can change with age and with each relationship.

The statements here were written for cv.cm and are inspired by Lee's model; this is not the published Love Attitudes Scale. Your result names your strongest style and shows your scores for all six. Different styles can work well together once partners understand each other.

faq.q: What are the six love styles?
faq.a: Eros (passionate, romantic love), Ludus (love as a playful game), Storge (love that grows from friendship), Pragma (practical, well-matched love), Mania (intense, anxious love) and Agape (selfless, giving love).

faq.q: Is one love style the best?
faq.a: No single style is best. Studies link Eros and Agape with more satisfying relationships and Mania with more jealousy and worry, but what matters most is that partners understand each other's style.

faq.q: Is this the same as love languages?
faq.a: No. Love languages are about how you like to give and receive affection. Love styles are about how you approach love itself: how fast you fall, what you look for and how intense it feels.

faq.q: Can my love style change?
faq.a: Yes. Lee saw the styles as attitudes, not fixed traits. They shift with experience, age and the partner you're with.

agape.name: Agape: selfless love

marriage.description: Are you ready for marriage? Free 20-question quiz on communication, conflict, money, family and shared goals, with a score for each area and a tip for the weakest. No sign-up.

Take it separately with your partner and compare. The area where your scores differ most is the best topic for your next long conversation.

faq.q: Should my partner take it too?

faq.q: What if we score low?
faq.a: A low score is a list of topics, not a verdict. Many couples work through them with honest talks or premarital counseling.

faq.q: Can married couples use it?
faq.a: Yes. The same five areas matter at every stage of a relationship.

tips.family: Discuss which family traditions and visits matter most to each of you, and present a united front to relatives.

conflict-style.title: Free conflict style test: how do you handle disagreements? — cv.cm
conflict-style.description: Free conflict style quiz. Rate 20 statements to see whether you lean toward competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding or accommodating, and when each style helps or hurts.
conflict-style.lede: Everyone has a default move when a disagreement starts. Find yours among the five classic conflict styles, see how strongly you use the others, and learn when to switch.
about: Researchers describe five ways of handling conflict along two questions: how hard you push for your own needs (assertiveness) and how much you care about the other person's (cooperativeness). Competing is high on the first, accommodating high on the second, collaborating high on both, avoiding low on both, and compromising sits in the middle.

The statements on this page were written for cv.cm; they are not taken from any commercial instrument. Every style is useful in the right moment. The aim is not to find the "right" style but to notice your habit and choose on purpose.

faq.q: What are the five conflict styles?
faq.a: Competing (stand your ground), collaborating (solve it together so both win), compromising (meet in the middle), avoiding (step away) and accommodating (give the other person what they want).

faq.q: Which conflict style is best?
faq.a: None in every case. Collaborating suits important issues with time to talk; competing suits emergencies; compromising suits deadlocks; avoiding suits trivial or heated moments; accommodating suits issues that matter more to the other side.

faq.q: Is this the Thomas-Kilmann instrument?
faq.a: No. It uses the same widely taught five-style model, but the questions and results are original to cv.cm, and the scores are not comparable to any commercial test.

faq.q: Can I use it with my partner or team?
faq.a: Yes. Take it separately, compare charts, and talk about which styles you each fall back on under stress. Knowing the other person's default makes it easier not to take it personally.

Try: before arguing, ask one genuine question about what the other person needs, and save full force for issues that truly matter.

collab.name: Collaborating
collab.body: You want a solution that fully works for both sides, and you dig into the real interests behind each position. Helps: important decisions, long-term relationships, problems with room for creative answers. Hurts: it takes time and energy, and not every small issue deserves a workshop. Try: decide up front whether a topic is worth the full process; for minor ones, a quick compromise is fine.

compromise.name: Compromising
compromise.body: You look for a fair middle so everyone can move on. Helps: deadlocks, equal power on both sides, time pressure. Hurts: splitting the difference too fast can leave both people half-satisfied and miss a better answer. Try: before offering the middle, ask "What matters most to you here?"; you may find a trade where each side gets what it cares about most.

avoid.name: Avoiding
avoid.body: You step back from conflict, and you're good at not escalating small things. Helps: trivial issues, heated moments that need a cool-down, fights you can't win or don't need to. Hurts: important problems grow while they wait, and others may read silence as agreement. Try: when you avoid, set a time to return ("Can we talk tomorrow evening?"), and write down the one point you need to make.

accommodate.name: Accommodating
accommodate.body: You protect the relationship and let others have their way. Helps: issues that matter more to them, when you realize you're wrong, building goodwill. Try: before saying yes, rate how much the issue matters to you from 1 to 10; above 6, say what you want, kindly and clearly.

faq.q: What is a Holland code?
faq.a: Your three strongest interest types, in order, such as SAE or RIC. It is used by career counselors to suggest fitting jobs and fields of study.

faq.q: Should I rate activities I have never tried?
faq.a: Yes. Imagine doing the activity and rate how much you would enjoy it, not how good you would be at it.

faq.q: Does this test measure talent?
faq.a: No. It measures interest. Skills can be learned; interest predicts which work you will enjoy long enough to get good at.

faq.q: My scores are almost equal. What now?
faq.a: A flat profile means broad interests. Look at careers that combine your top types, and try short projects to see what you enjoy.

about: Job satisfaction depends not only on what you do but on how the work is set up. Each score runs from 0 to 100. Below 40 leans one way, above 60 the other, and the middle is a mix. Use the result to ask better questions in job interviews ("How many days are in the office?", "How are priorities set?") and to shape the job you have.

faq.q: Does this tell me which career to choose?

faq.q: My remote score is in the middle. What does that mean?
faq.a: You'll probably be happiest in a hybrid setup: office days for meetings and people, home days for focused work.

faq.q: What if my job doesn't match my result?
faq.a: Small changes help: block focus time on your calendar, ask for one remote day, agree on clearer priorities with your manager, or swap tasks with a teammate who likes the work you don't.

faq.q: Is one work style better than another?
faq.a: No. Teams need both people who like structure and people who like freedom, both soloists and connectors. What matters is fit.

team.mid: Mixed: you like time alone to do the work and time together to plan and review it. Batch meetings into one part of the day and keep the rest for focus.
team.high: Team: you think best out loud and enjoy shared goals. Look for collaborative roles such as project work, sales, teaching or product teams, and on solo tasks, pair up or hold short check-ins to stay motivated.

structure.low: Freedom: you want to decide how and when to work. Startups, freelancing and roles judged on results suit you. Set your own deadlines and share them, so freedom doesn't turn into last-minute stress.
structure.mid: Balanced: you like clear goals but some say in how to reach them. Ask managers for the "what" and "by when", and propose the "how" yourself.
structure.high: Structure: clear expectations, processes and priorities calm you and help you do excellent work. Larger organizations and process-driven roles suit you; when things are vague, ask early for a checklist or definition of done.

variety.low: Deep focus: you do your best work in long, uninterrupted blocks. Book two- or three-hour focus blocks, turn off notifications, and look for roles that value depth such as research, engineering or editing.
variety.mid: Balanced: some variety keeps you fresh, but too much switching wears you down. Group similar tasks together and give each day one main focus.
variety.high: Variety: new problems and a fast pace energize you, and routine bores you. Roles in operations, client work, events or startups fit; keep a simple list so many threads don't slip.

leadership.title: Free leadership style test: which of the 6 styles are you? — cv.cm
leadership.description: Free leadership style quiz based on Goleman's six styles: visionary, coaching, affiliative, democratic, pacesetting and commanding. Rate 24 statements to see your main style and when to use the others.
leadership.lede: How do you lead when it's your call? Rate 24 statements to find your main style among the six described by Daniel Goleman, and when each style helps or hurts a team.
about: In 2000 the psychologist Daniel Goleman described six leadership styles based on research with thousands of managers: visionary, coaching, affiliative, democratic, pacesetting and commanding. The best leaders don't stick to one; they switch styles to fit the situation, as a golfer picks a club.

The statements here were written for cv.cm and are inspired by Goleman's model. Your result shows your strongest style and your scores for all six. You don't need a manager's title to use it: leading a project, a club or a group of friends counts.

faq.q: What are the six leadership styles?
faq.a: Visionary (sets a direction and lets people find the way), coaching (develops people), affiliative (puts people and harmony first), democratic (builds agreement), pacesetting (sets high standards by example) and commanding (gives clear orders).

faq.q: Which leadership style is best?
faq.a: Goleman's research found that visionary, coaching, affiliative and democratic styles usually improve a team's climate, while pacesetting and commanding work in short bursts, such as a crisis or a skilled team on a deadline, but wear people down if overused.

faq.q: I'm not a manager. Is this test for me?
faq.a: Yes. Answer as you act when you lead anything: a school project, a team at work, an event or a trip with friends.

faq.q: How can I widen my range?
faq.a: Pick the style you scored lowest that would help your team, and try it on purpose for a few weeks: for example, ask for ideas before you decide, or set aside time to coach one person.

coaching.body: You lead by developing people: you ask about their goals, give useful feedback and make time to teach. It builds strong, loyal teams over time. It works less well when people don't want to learn, or when the deadline is tomorrow.

affiliative.name: Affiliative leader
affiliative.body: You lead by putting people first, building harmony, trust and team spirit. It's ideal for healing a team after conflict or keeping morale up under stress. Pair it with clear goals and honest feedback, so poor work doesn't go unaddressed.

democratic.name: Democratic leader
democratic.body: You lead by listening and building agreement, so people feel ownership of decisions. It works well when you need fresh ideas or buy-in. In a crisis, or when the team is stuck in endless meetings, be ready to make the call.

pacesetting.name: Pacesetting leader
pacesetting.body: You lead by example and set high standards for speed and quality. It gets fast results from a skilled, motivated team. Used too long it can overwhelm people, so explain the why, share the load and recognise effort.

commanding.name: Commanding leader
commanding.body: You lead by taking control and giving clear instructions. In a real emergency or a turnaround, that decisiveness is exactly what's needed. Used every day it can stifle people, so loosen control once things are stable and ask for input.

mindset.title: Growth mindset test: do you have a fixed or growth mindset? — cv.cm
mindset.description: Free growth mindset quiz inspired by Carol Dweck's research: rate 10 statements about talent, effort and mistakes to see whether you lean toward a fixed or a growth mindset. Takes 2 minutes.
mindset.lede: Do you believe talent is set at birth or that it grows with practice? Rate 10 statements to see where you sit between a fixed and a growth mindset, and how to move toward growth.
about: The psychologist Carol Dweck of Stanford University found that people differ in what they believe about ability. With a fixed mindset, intelligence and talent are things you either have or don't, so mistakes feel like proof of your limits. With a growth mindset, abilities develop through effort, good strategies and help from others, so mistakes are information.

The statements here were written for cv.cm and inspired by Dweck's work; half describe a growth view and half a fixed one. Your score runs from 0 (strongly fixed) to 40 (strongly growth). Nobody has a pure growth mindset all the time, and mindsets can change with practice.

faq.q: What is the difference between a fixed and a growth mindset?
faq.a: A fixed mindset sees talent and intelligence as set; a growth mindset sees them as abilities that develop with effort, strategy and feedback. The difference shows most when things get hard.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement is scored 0 to 4. Growth statements count as you agree; fixed statements count as you disagree. The total runs from 0 to 40: 13 or less leans fixed, 14 to 26 is mixed, 27 or more leans growth.

faq.q: Can I change my mindset?
faq.a: Yes. Notice fixed-mindset thoughts ("I'm just not a math person"), add "yet" to them, treat mistakes as feedback, and praise effort and strategy rather than talent, in yourself and in others.

faq.q: Does a growth mindset guarantee success?
faq.a: No. Later studies found its effects on grades are real but often small, and bigger for struggling students. It helps most when combined with good teaching, effective strategies and support.

mixed.body: Like most people, you see growth in some areas and fixed limits in others. Notice which situations trigger a fixed view, such as failure, criticism or a talented rival, and practice treating those moments as feedback rather than verdicts.

growth.body: You see ability as something that grows with effort and good strategies, and you're likely to take on challenges and learn from setbacks. Keep pairing effort with new strategies and asking for help, and share that outlook with the people around you.

about: Financial psychologists such as Brad Klontz describe money beliefs we absorb growing up, which quietly drive how we save, spend and invest. This quiz, written for cv.cm, sorts common habits into five money personalities.
No type is good or bad. Each has a strength to use and a blind spot to manage. This quiz cannot predict your fortune: it describes habits, and habits can change.

faq.q: Can this test predict how rich I will be?
faq.a: No. No test can predict fortune. It shows habits that tend to help or hurt your finances over time, which you can change.

faq.q: What are the five money types here?
faq.a: Saver, spender, investor (risk-taker), avoider, and giver.

faq.q: Can I be more than one type?
faq.a: Yes. The chart shows all five. Many people are, for example, a saver with a strong giver side.

faq.q: What should couples do with their results?
faq.a: Compare types. A saver and a spender together can balance each other if they agree on a shared budget.

spender.name: The Spender
spender.body: Strength: you enjoy life and are generous with experiences. Blind spot: impulse buys and little left for the future. Tip: move a fixed amount to savings automatically on payday, and wait 48 hours before any non-essential purchase.

investor.name: The Investor
investor.body: Strength: you spot opportunities and let money work for you. Blind spot: chasing big wins can mean too much risk in one place. Tip: keep an emergency fund first, and never put more into one bet than you can afford to lose.

avoider.name: The Avoider
avoider.body: Strength: money doesn't run your life. Blind spot: unopened bills, late fees and missed chances because looking feels stressful. Tip: book a 15-minute money date each week to check your balance and pay bills; it gets easier fast.

giver.name: The Giver
giver.body: Strength: generosity and strong relationships. Blind spot: giving away what you need for your own security. Tip: decide on a giving budget in advance, so you can be generous without putting your own future at risk.

chronotype.title: Free chronotype test: are you a morning lark or a night owl? — cv.cm
chronotype.description: Free chronotype quiz. Answer 14 questions about your natural sleep and energy rhythm to see if you are a morning lark, a night owl or in between, with practical schedule tips.
chronotype.h1: Chronotype test: morning lark or night owl?
chronotype.lede: Your chronotype is your body clock's natural timing: when you feel sleepy, when you wake, and when you think best. Answer 14 questions about how you live when nobody sets the alarm.
about: Chronotype is partly genetic and changes with age: teenagers and young adults tend to run late, and most people shift earlier after their mid-twenties. Larks feel sharpest in the morning; owls hit their stride in the evening; most people are somewhere in between.

The questions here were written for cv.cm and are not a clinical questionnaire. The result is a self-reflection, not a diagnosis. If you often can't fall asleep, wake up exhausted after a full night, or feel very sleepy during the day, talk to a doctor: those can be signs of a sleep problem that has nothing to do with being an owl.

faq.q: Can a night owl become a morning person?
faq.a: Partly. Your underlying tendency stays, but you can shift your schedule earlier with steady habits: bright light soon after waking, dim light in the evening, and the same wake time every day, moved 15 minutes at a time.

faq.q: Is one chronotype healthier?
faq.a: No chronotype is unhealthy by itself. Problems come from a mismatch: an owl forced into early starts builds up sleep debt. Matching your schedule to your clock where you can, and keeping it regular, matters most.

faq.q: Why do you ask about weekends?
faq.a: Sleeping much later on free days than on workdays, sometimes called social jet lag, is a common sign that your natural clock runs later than your schedule.

faq.q: Is this a sleep disorder test?
faq.a: No. It describes your natural timing. It cannot detect insomnia, sleep apnea or other conditions; see a doctor if sleep problems affect your daily life.

Tips: put your hardest work between about 8 a.m. and noon and keep afternoons for meetings and routine tasks; protect your bedtime on nights out, or plan a short afternoon nap instead of a late lie-in; dim screens an hour before bed so you don't wake at 4 a.m. Larks often find late-evening social life tiring: it's fine to suggest brunch instead of drinks.

between.body: Your clock sits in the middle, like most people's, so you adapt fairly easily to normal schedules. A steady routine matters more than which hour you choose.

owl.body: Your body clock runs late: mornings are hard and you come alive in the evening. pet.title: Which pet is right for me? Free pet match quiz — cv.cm
pet.description: Free pet quiz. Answer 14 questions about your time, home, budget, allergies and lifestyle to see whether a cat, dog, rabbit, fish, bird, hamster or reptile suits you best.
pet.lede: A good match makes life better for you and the animal. Answer 14 honest questions about your time, space, money and habits, and see which pet fits your life right now.
about: This quiz, written for cv.cm, weighs the practical things that decide whether an animal will thrive with you: daily time, home size, hours away, travel, allergies, budget, noise, lifespan and the chores you can live with. It is a starting point, not a guarantee: individual animals and breeds vary a lot.

Before you bring any animal home: research the species' needs, count the full cost including vet care, check your lease and local rules, and think about who will care for it when you travel. Consider adopting from a shelter or rescue, and fostering first if you're unsure. A pet is a commitment for its whole life, which can mean decades.

faq.q: What is the easiest pet for a beginner?
faq.a: There is no zero-effort pet. For busy people, a cat or a properly set-up aquarium usually fits best; for families with time and space, a dog. Small animals like hamsters and rabbits need more specialized care than people expect.

faq.q: I'm allergic. Can I still have a pet?
faq.a: Fish and reptiles don't shed fur or dander, so they are the safest choices. No cat or dog is truly hypoallergenic; if you want one, spend time with that animal before adopting and ask a doctor.

faq.q: How much does a pet cost?
faq.a: It depends on the species and where you live. Beyond food, plan for the setup (cage, tank, lamps), vaccinations, neutering, and an emergency vet fund. Reptile and aquarium setups cost more up front than many people expect.

faq.q: Should I get a pet for my child?
faq.a: Only if an adult is ready to be the real caregiver. Children can help, but hamsters and rabbits are fragile and often don't like being held, so supervise every interaction.

cat.name: Cat
cat.body: A cat fits a busy life with moderate space: independent but affectionate, fine alone during a workday, no walks needed. Plan for: 15 or more years, a clean litter box (one per cat plus one), scratching posts, play every day, yearly vet checks, and neutering. Indoor cats live longer; a catio or window perch keeps them entertained.

dog.name: Dog
dog.body: You have the time, space and energy a dog needs, and you want a companion who shares your days. Plan for: 10 to 15 years, walks and play every day, training from day one, someone home or a dog walker on long days, and a bigger budget for food, grooming and vets. Choose energy level and size to match your life, and look at shelters and breed rescues first.

rabbit.name: Rabbit
rabbit.body: A rabbit suits a calm home with floor space and someone around much of the day. Rabbits are social, so most are happiest in a bonded pair, and they need hours of free-roam time in a rabbit-proofed room, not a small hutch. Plan for: 8 to 12 years, unlimited hay, a vet who knows rabbits, and neutering. They rarely enjoy being picked up; enjoy them on their level.

fish.name: Fish
fish.body: An aquarium fits small spaces, tight schedules and allergies, and it's genuinely calming to watch. Skip the bowl: start with a filtered, heated tank of at least 40 liters (about 10 gallons), and cycle it for several weeks before adding fish. Plan for: weekly partial water changes, testing kits, and choosing species that suit the tank size and each other.

bird.name: Bird
bird.body: A bird fits someone home a lot who enjoys interaction and doesn't mind noise. Parrots, even small ones, are smart, social and need hours of time outside the cage, toys to chew and training. Plan for: a long life (budgies 5 to 10 years, larger parrots 30 or more), an avian vet, and a fresh diet beyond seed. If you're away all day, a pair of small birds may be better than one.

hamster.name: Hamster
hamster.body: A hamster fits a small space, a modest budget and a quiet evening routine. They are solitary and nocturnal, so they'll be awake when you're winding down, and their wheel may squeak at night. Plan for: a big enclosure (at least 100 × 50 cm floor), deep bedding to burrow, a solid wheel of the right size, and a 2- to 3-year life. Handle gently; they're not ideal for young children.

reptile.name: Reptile
reptile.body: A reptile fits someone who is curious, patient, allergic to fur, or away often. Many species are quiet and fine alone for a day or two once their setup runs well. Plan for: a proper enclosure with heat and UVB lighting on timers, live or frozen food for many species, an exotic-animal vet, and a long life (leopard geckos 15 to 20 years, tortoises much longer). Choose captive-bred animals and research the species first.

Most faces are a mix of two shapes, so the quiz also shows how close you are to each. Face shape is about proportions, not beauty: every shape has styles that flatter it.

faq.q: How do I measure my face shape?
faq.a: Measure forehead width at the hairline, cheekbone width at the widest point, jaw width from the corner under each ear to the chin, and length from hairline to chin. Then answer the questions.

faq.q: What is the most common face shape?
faq.a: Oval and round are often cited as the most common, but many people are a blend of two shapes.

faq.q: Does the test use my photo?
faq.a: No. You answer from a mirror or your own photo; nothing is uploaded or analyzed.

faq.q: Can makeup or a beard change my face shape?

wellbeing-index.title: Free well-being test (WHO-5 Well-Being Index): score 0–100 — cv.cm
wellbeing-index.description: Free WHO-5 well-being test online. Answer 5 questions about the last two weeks to get your well-being score from 0 to 100 and what it means. Private: nothing leaves your browser.
wellbeing-index.lede: The WHO-5 Well-Being Index asks 5 short questions about how you have felt over the last two weeks. It takes under a minute and gives a score from 0 to 100.
about: The WHO-5 was published by the World Health Organization Regional Office for Europe in 1998 and is one of the most widely used well-being questionnaires in the world. It is free to use. Each answer scores 0 to 5; the total (0–25) is multiplied by 4 to give a percentage from 0 (worst possible) to 100 (best possible).
A score below 52 suggests poor well-being, and doctors use it as a reason to check for depression; a score of 28 or less often goes with depression. This test is a self-check, not a diagnosis.

faq.q: What does my WHO-5 score mean?
faq.a: Multiply the raw score (0–25) by 4. 52 or more is in the normal range of well-being. Below 52 suggests poor well-being. 28 or less is a sign that depression may be present and should be checked by a professional.

faq.q: Is the WHO-5 a depression test?
faq.a: It measures positive well-being, not depression symptoms, but a low score is a good reason to screen for depression, for example with the PHQ-9 test on this site, and to talk to a doctor.

faq.q: How often can I take it?
faq.a: It asks about the last two weeks, so retaking it every two weeks or so is a simple way to track how you're doing. A change of 10 points or more is considered meaningful.

faq.q: What can improve my well-being?
faq.a: Regular sleep, daylight and movement, time with people you like, and doing things that interest you help many people. If a low mood lasts, talk to a doctor or counselor.

self-esteem.title: Free self-esteem test (Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale) — cv.cm
self-esteem.description: Take the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale online for free. 10 statements, an instant score out of 30 and what it means. No sign-up, answers stay in your browser.
self-esteem.lede: The Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale is the most widely used measure of self-worth. Rate 10 statements and get a score out of 30.
about: Sociologist Morris Rosenberg published the scale in 1965, and it has been used in thousands of studies since. Five statements are positive and five are negative; the negative ones are reverse-scored.
Scores from 15 to 25 are in the typical range. A score below 15 suggests low self-esteem. Self-esteem changes with life events, and it can be built with practice and support.

faq.q: How is the Rosenberg scale scored?
faq.a: Each answer scores 0 to 3, with items 2, 5, 6, 8 and 9 reversed. The total runs from 0 to 30; higher means higher self-esteem.

faq.q: What is a normal score?
faq.a: Most people score between 15 and 25. Below 15 suggests low self-esteem.

faq.q: How can I improve my self-esteem?
faq.a: Notice and challenge harsh self-talk, keep small promises to yourself, spend time with supportive people, and talk to a counselor if low self-worth affects daily life.

faq.q: Is a high score always good?
faq.a: Healthy self-esteem is realistic. A very high score is usually fine, but self-worth that depends on always being better than others is fragile.

anxiety.description: Free GAD-7 anxiety test online. Answer 7 questions about the last two weeks and get your score from 0 to 21 with the standard severity level. Private: nothing leaves your browser.
anxiety.lede: The GAD-7 is a 7-question screening tool doctors use to check for generalized anxiety. It takes about a minute and scores from 0 to 21.
about: The Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7) was developed by Spitzer, Kroenke, Williams and Löwe in 2006. It is free to use and is widely used in primary care. Scores of 5, 10 and 15 mark mild, moderate and severe anxiety.
A score of 10 or more is a reason to talk to a doctor or mental health professional. This check is a screening tool, not a diagnosis.

faq.q: What does my GAD-7 score mean?
faq.a: 0–4 minimal, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate and 15–21 severe anxiety symptoms over the last two weeks.

faq.q: Can the GAD-7 diagnose anxiety disorder?
faq.a: No. It screens for symptoms. A diagnosis needs an assessment by a qualified professional.

faq.q: When should I seek help?
faq.a: If your score is 10 or more, or if anxiety gets in the way of work, school, sleep or relationships, talk to a doctor or counselor.

faq.q: What helps with anxiety?
faq.a: Regular sleep, exercise, less caffeine, slow breathing and talking to someone you trust help many people. Therapy (such as CBT) and medication are effective treatments.

depression.lede: The PHQ-9 is the 9-question depression screening used by doctors worldwide. It takes about two minutes and scores from 0 to 27.
about: The Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) was developed by Kroenke, Spitzer and Williams and is free to use. Scores of 5, 10, 15 and 20 mark mild, moderate, moderately severe and severe depression symptoms.
A score of 10 or more is a reason to see a doctor or mental health professional. If you have any thoughts of hurting yourself, reach out for help now, whatever your total score.

faq.q: What does my PHQ-9 score mean?
faq.a: 0–4 minimal, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 moderately severe and 20–27 severe depression symptoms.

faq.q: Can the PHQ-9 diagnose depression?
faq.a: No. It is a screening tool. A doctor or mental health professional makes a diagnosis after a full assessment.

faq.q: Why does question 9 matter so much?
faq.a: It asks about thoughts of death or self-harm. Any answer other than "not at all" deserves a conversation with a professional, even if the total score is low.

faq.q: Is depression treatable?
faq.a: Yes. Therapy, medication, exercise and social support all help, and most people improve with treatment.

tails.name: Miles "Tails" Prower
tails.body: Clever, loyal and always building something. You solve problems with your head, stick by your best friend and are braver than you think.

knuckles.name: Knuckles the Echidna
knuckles.body: Strong, honest and protective. You take your duties seriously and will guard what matters with everything you have, even if you sometimes trust the wrong person.

amy.name: Amy Rose
amy.body: Cheerful, determined and full of heart. You know what you want and chase it without giving up, and you stay optimistic when everyone else has stopped believing.

shadow.name: Shadow the Hedgehog
shadow.body: Serious, intense and driven by purpose. You keep your feelings to yourself and work best alone, but you never forget a promise.

rouge.name: Rouge the Bat
rouge.body: Stylish, witty and good at getting what you want. You like nice things and a bit of danger, and under the teasing you are a better friend than you let on.

cream.name: Cream the Rabbit
cream.body: Sweet, polite and kind. You treat everyone with good manners, love a quiet afternoon with friends and are steadier than people expect.

silver.name: Silver the Hedgehog
silver.body: Earnest, idealistic and always thinking ahead. You want to fix what is broken and change how the future turns out, even if you are a little naive about how.

faq.q: What are the 12 D&D classes?
faq.a: Barbarian, bard, cleric, druid, fighter, monk, paladin, ranger, rogue, sorcerer, warlock and wizard. Some editions and books add more, such as the artificer.

faq.q: What is the difference between a sorcerer, a warlock and a wizard?
faq.a: A wizard learns magic through study, a sorcerer is born with it, and a warlock gets it from a pact with a powerful patron.

faq.q: Which D&D class is best for beginners?
faq.a: Fighter and barbarian are the simplest to play, and a cleric is a good start if you'd like some spells. Pick the class that sounds fun: you'll learn it faster.

faq.q: Is this an official D&D quiz?

barbarian.name: Barbarian
barbarian.body: Bold, direct and full of energy. You act on instinct, say what you think and are the first one through the door. Your strength is real, and so is your loyalty to your party.

bard.name: Bard
bard.body: Charming, creative and the life of the party. You solve problems with words and wit, collect stories everywhere you go and make every group better.

cleric.name: Cleric
cleric.body: Caring, faithful and steady. You hold the group together, heal what is hurt and draw strength from something bigger than yourself.

druid.name: Druid
druid.body: Calm, wise and connected to nature. You feel most at home outdoors, think in long cycles and protect the balance others forget about.

fighter.name: Fighter
fighter.body: Disciplined, practical and dependable. You train, plan and hold the line. No flash, just reliable skill that keeps everyone alive.

monk.name: Monk
monk.body: Focused, patient and self-disciplined. You value balance and inner calm, and when you do act, you are faster than anyone expects.

paladin.name: Paladin
paladin.body: Principled, brave and protective. You live by a code, stand up for people who can't defend themselves and keep your promises even when it costs you.

ranger.name: Ranger
ranger.body: Independent, observant and at home in the wild. You notice what others miss, prefer open country to crowded cities and are deadly accurate when it counts.

rogue.name: Rogue
rogue.body: Clever, quick and independent. You read a room in seconds, find the back way in and value your freedom more than anyone's rules.

sorcerer.name: Sorcerer
sorcerer.body: Gifted, expressive and a little unpredictable. Your talent comes naturally and runs on emotion, and learning to control it is your life's adventure.

warlock.name: Warlock
warlock.body: Mysterious, curious and ambitious. You are drawn to secrets and hidden knowledge, and you're willing to make bold bargains to get what you want.

wizard.name: Wizard
wizard.body: Curious, analytical and always studying. You believe the right knowledge solves any problem, and you'll happily spend all night reading to find it.

hinata.name: Hinata Hyuga
hinata.body: Gentle, shy and braver than anyone realizes. You cheer for others quietly, keep growing in your own way and stand firm when it really counts.

shikamaru.name: Shikamaru Nara

gaara.name: Gaara
gaara.body: Quiet, protective and deeply understanding. You know loneliness from the inside, which is why you look out for others and try to understand people before judging them.

itachi.name: Itachi Uchiha
itachi.body: Calm, gifted and hard to read. You never raise your voice, think several moves ahead and keep your feelings to yourself. People rarely see how much you carry.

lee.name: Rock Lee

jiraiya.name: Jiraiya
jiraiya.body: Free-spirited, funny and wise. You've seen a lot of the world, you teach through stories and you believe in the next generation more than they believe in themselves.

zoro.name: Roronoa Zoro

nami.body: Smart, sharp and always three steps ahead, especially where money's involved. You plan the route everyone else follows, and under the tough exterior you'd do anything for the people you call home.

about: DISC describes four styles of behavior: Dominance (direct, results first), Influence (outgoing, persuasive), Steadiness (patient, supportive) and Conscientiousness (accurate, careful). The model goes back to the psychologist William Moulton Marston, who described four patterns of emotion and behavior in his 1928 book Emotions of Normal People. Others later turned his ideas into workplace questionnaires.

The statements here were written for cv.cm. This is not Everything DiSC or any other commercial assessment and has no link to their publishers; DiSC is a registered trademark of its owner. DISC is widely used in training but is less well supported by research than the Big Five, so use your result to start a conversation, not to make hiring decisions.

faq.q: What do the four DISC letters stand for?
faq.a: D is Dominance, I is Influence, S is Steadiness and C is Conscientiousness. Some versions use slightly different words, but the four styles are much the same.

faq.q: How is the DISC result worked out?
faq.a: Each style has five statements, scored 0 to 4. Your result is the style with the highest score, and the bars show all four. If two styles tie, the page names both.

faq.q: Which DISC style is best?
faq.a: None. D gets things moving, I brings people along, S keeps a team steady and C keeps the quality high. Good teams need all four, and most people use more than one.

faq.q: Is this the official DiSC assessment?
faq.a: No. It is a free, independent test based on the same public idea. Commercial reports are longer and have their own scoring, so your result there may differ.

highly-sensitive-person.description: Free highly sensitive person (HSP) test: rate 14 statements on noise, crowds, emotions and detail to get a score from 0 to 56 and what it means. Not a diagnosis. Answers stay in your browser.
highly-sensitive-person.lede: Do loud rooms wear you out? Do you notice small changes, and feel other people's moods? Rate 14 statements to see how sensitive you are, and how to look after yourself if the answer is very.
about: The psychologists Elaine Aron and Arthur Aron introduced the term highly sensitive person in the 1990s to describe people with high sensory processing sensitivity: they notice more and take in what they notice more deeply, so they can also get overwhelmed sooner. Aron estimated that 15–20% of people are highly sensitive; a 2018 study by Lionetti and colleagues put the most sensitive group nearer 30%.

High sensitivity is a personality trait, not a disorder. The statements here were written for cv.cm; this is not Aron's HSP Scale, and half of them describe low sensitivity so that simply agreeing with everything doesn't raise your score. Our score bands are a rough guide, not research cut-offs.

faq.q: What does it mean to be a highly sensitive person?
faq.a: You react more strongly to what's around you: noise, light, crowds, art and other people's feelings. That can make you perceptive and empathetic, and also quicker to tire in busy places.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, and half are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 56. 18 or less is low sensitivity, 19 to 37 is medium, and 38 or more is high.

faq.q: Is being an HSP the same as being introverted or anxious?
faq.a: No. Many highly sensitive people are introverted, but a good share are extroverted. Sensitivity is about how deeply you process things; anxiety is about worry and fear. If worry is what troubles you, try the GAD-7 anxiety check on this site.

faq.q: Is high sensitivity a disorder?
faq.a: No. It is a normal variation in temperament and isn't a medical diagnosis. If you feel overwhelmed most of the time or it stops you living your life, talk to a doctor or therapist.

about: Narcissism is a personality trait that everyone has to some degree. It runs from healthy self-confidence to a strong need for admiration, a sense of entitlement and little interest in other people's feelings. Psychologists have measured it since Raskin and Hall's Narcissistic Personality Inventory in 1979.

The statements here were written for cv.cm and are not a clinical instrument. Half are reversed, so agreeing with everything doesn't raise your score. Narcissistic personality disorder is a rare condition that only a qualified professional can diagnose, and a high score here doesn't mean you have it. This test is about you: it isn't meant for labeling a partner, a parent or anybody else.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, half reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 64. 21 or less is low, 22 to 42 is medium, and 43 or more is high. The bands are a guide for this test, not clinical cut-offs.

faq.q: Is some narcissism healthy?
faq.a: Yes. Confidence, ambition and enjoying recognition are normal. Problems start when the need for admiration comes at other people's expense or when any criticism feels unbearable.

faq.q: What if someone close to me behaves like a narcissist?
faq.a: A quiz taken on someone else's behalf can't tell you much. Focus on the behavior and how it affects you. If you feel controlled, belittled or unsafe, talk to someone you trust, a counselor or a local support service.

about: The World Health Organization's ICD-11 describes burnout as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition. It results from chronic workplace stress that hasn't been successfully managed and has three dimensions: exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism about your job, and reduced effectiveness at work.

The statements here were written for cv.cm around those three dimensions. This isn't the Maslach Burnout Inventory, and it hasn't been clinically validated, so the score bands are a rough guide rather than clinical cut-offs. Depression, thyroid problems and other medical conditions can feel like burnout. If you feel this way most of the time, see a doctor. If you study or care for someone rather than work a job, answer with that in mind.

faq.q: What are the signs of burnout?
faq.a: The three main signs are feeling drained, feeling negative or detached about your job, and getting less done or doubting your ability. Poor sleep, headaches and irritability often come along with them.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, and half are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 64. 21 or less is low, 22 to 42 suggests some risk, and 43 or more suggests strong signs of burnout.

faq.q: What is the difference between burnout and depression?
faq.a: Burnout is tied to work, while depression usually affects all of life, including things you normally enjoy. They overlap, and one can lead to the other. If your low mood goes beyond work, try the PHQ-9 check on this site and talk to a doctor.

faq.q: How do I recover from burnout?
faq.a: Rest helps, but it rarely lasts unless the cause changes too. Look at your workload, your control over it, how you're treated and whether you get enough time off. Talk to your manager or occupational health service if you can, and see a doctor if symptoms persist.

about: ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) is a neurodevelopmental condition that starts in childhood and often continues into adult life. It shows up as lasting problems with attention, restlessness or impulsivity. A diagnosis needs a professional assessment: symptoms must have begun in childhood, show up in more than one area of life and cause real problems.

These statements were written for cv.cm around those symptom areas. This isn't the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) and it hasn't been clinically validated, so it can't screen for or rule out ADHD, and its bands aren't clinical cut-offs. Use it to organize your thoughts before seeing a professional, who may use a validated tool such as the ASRS. Poor sleep, stress, anxiety, depression and other conditions can cause similar problems.

faq.q: Can this test tell me if I have ADHD?
faq.a: No. Only a qualified professional can diagnose ADHD, after asking about your history, including childhood, and ruling out other causes. A high score is simply a reason to ask, and a low score doesn't rule it out.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, so the total runs from 0 to 72. 28 or less counts as few signs, 29 to 47 as some and 48 or more as many. The bands are a guide for this test only, not clinical cut-offs.

faq.q: Is this the ASRS?
faq.a: No. The ASRS is a separate validated questionnaire whose wording can't be changed. Our statements are original and have not been validated, so a clinician may ask you to fill in the ASRS or a similar tool.

faq.q: What else can look like ADHD?
faq.a: Lack of sleep, anxiety, depression, stress, thyroid problems, some medicines and heavy phone use can all harm attention. That's why a professional checks for other causes.

stress.lede: Feeling stretched thin, on edge or out of control? Rate 14 statements about the past month to see how stressed you have been, and what can help.
about: Stress is the body's response to pressure. In short bursts it can sharpen you, but when demands keep feeling bigger than your ability to cope, it wears you down: poor sleep, irritability, worry, tension and trouble concentrating are common signs. Psychologists often measure perceived stress, meaning how unpredictable, uncontrollable and overloaded your life feels, rather than counting stressful events.

The statements here were written for cv.cm around common signs of stress in the body, sleep, mood, thinking and habits. They are not taken from the Perceived Stress Scale or any other questionnaire, and they haven't been clinically validated, so the score bands are a rough guide rather than clinical cut-offs. Half the statements are reversed, so agreeing with everything lands in the middle. If stress is affecting your health, sleep or relationships for weeks, talk to a doctor or counselor.

faq.q: How is the stress score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4 and half are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 56. 18 or less is low, 19 to 37 is moderate and 38 or more is high.

faq.q: What are the signs of too much stress?
faq.a: Common signs are trouble sleeping, feeling tense or irritable, worrying a lot, headaches or an upset stomach, finding it hard to concentrate, and using alcohol, food or screens to cope.

faq.q: How can I lower my stress quickly?
faq.a: Slow breathing (breathe out for longer than you breathe in), a short walk, writing your worries down and picking one small next step all help in the moment. Over weeks, regular sleep, exercise, time with people you trust and cutting back on what you can control make the biggest difference.

faq.q: What is the difference between stress and anxiety?
faq.a: Stress is usually a reaction to a pressure you can name, such as a deadline, and eases when it passes. Anxiety is worry or fear that can continue without a clear cause. If worry stays with you most days, try the GAD-7 anxiety check on this site.

items: My shoulders, jaw or stomach have felt tense most days.

about: Learning style models sort people by how they prefer to take in information. A well-known version, Neil Fleming's VARK, uses four: visual (pictures, diagrams, charts), auditory (listening and talking), reading and writing (text, lists, notes) and kinesthetic (doing, examples and practice). This quiz uses the same four preferences.

The statements were written for cv.cm; this is not the VARK questionnaire and has no link to its authors. Research has found little evidence that people learn better when teaching is matched to their preferred style, so treat your result as a preference, not a limit. Most people learn best by mixing methods, and testing yourself and spacing out study sessions help whatever your style.

faq.q: What are the four learning styles?
faq.a: Visual (diagrams, charts and color), auditory (lectures, discussion and saying things out loud), reading and writing (text, lists and notes) and kinesthetic (hands-on practice, real examples and movement).

faq.q: Are learning styles real?
faq.a: People do have preferences, and this quiz measures them. What research does not support is the idea that you only learn well in your style. The material matters too: maps are best seen and languages are best heard and spoken.

faq.q: Can I have more than one learning style?
faq.a: Yes. Many people score highly on two or three. Your result names your strongest preference and shows your score for all four.

faq.q: How should I study for my learning style?
faq.a: Start with your preferred method to make material feel approachable, then add others. Whatever your result, quizzing yourself, explaining ideas in your own words and spreading study over several days work better than rereading.

kinesthetic.body: You learn by doing. Practice, real examples, experiments and movement make ideas click. Try worked problems, building models, role play or studying on your feet in short sessions. Connect each idea to something you've experienced, then test yourself on it.

about: The dark triad is a set of three overlapping personality traits named by psychologists Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams in 2002: Machiavellianism (strategic, manipulative, cynical about others), narcissism (a need for admiration and a sense of being special) and psychopathy (impulsive, thrill-seeking, low in empathy and guilt). Everyone has some of each; they are measured on a scale, like other traits.

The statements were written for cv.cm; this is not the Short Dark Triad (SD3) or any clinical tool. A high score is not a diagnosis of narcissistic or antisocial personality disorder, which only a clinician can make. Half the statements are reversed, so agreeing with everything lands in the middle. Use your result to reflect, not to label yourself or anyone else.

faq.q: What are the three dark triad traits?
faq.a: Machiavellianism is a cold, strategic approach to people and a willingness to manipulate them. Narcissism is grandiosity, entitlement and a need for admiration. Psychopathy is impulsivity, thrill-seeking and a lack of empathy or remorse.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each trait has six statements scored 0 to 4, three of them reversed, giving a score for each trait out of 24, shown as a percentage. Below 40% is low, 40–60% is average and above 60% is high.

faq.q: Does a high score mean I'm a psychopath?
faq.a: No. These are everyday traits that vary across the population, and a self-report quiz cannot diagnose a personality disorder. Moderate levels can even help in competitive settings; very high levels tend to harm relationships over time.

faq.q: Can I take it about someone else?
faq.a: It is written for rating yourself. Answering for a partner or coworker mostly measures your view of them, so don't use it to label people.

empath.lede: Do you feel other people's moods as if they were your own, and leave a sad conversation drained? Rate 14 statements to see how strongly you tune in to others, and how to look after yourself if the answer is very.
about: "Empath" is a popular word, not a scientific category, for someone who takes in other people's emotions very strongly. Psychologists study the same ground as empathy, which they usually split into two parts: affective empathy, feeling what someone else feels, and cognitive empathy, understanding what they feel and why. People differ a lot on both, and very high affective empathy can be tiring if you don't also have ways to step back.

The statements here were written for cv.cm around everyday signs of strong empathy. They are not taken from any published empathy scale, and half of them describe low empathy so that simply agreeing with everything lands in the middle. The score bands are a rough guide, not research cut-offs. Being an empath is not a diagnosis, and it is not a superpower either: it is one end of an ordinary human trait.

faq.q: What is an empath?
faq.a: Someone who senses and takes on other people's emotions very strongly, often before anyone says a word. The term comes from popular psychology; researchers would describe it as very high affective empathy.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, and half are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 56. 18 or less is low, 19 to 37 is in the middle, and 38 or more is high.

faq.q: Is an empath the same as a highly sensitive person?
faq.a: They overlap, but they are not the same. High sensitivity is about how deeply you process everything around you, including noise, light and detail; being an empath is about other people's feelings in particular. You can try the highly sensitive person test on this site too.

faq.q: How can empaths protect their energy?
faq.a: Notice which feelings are yours and which you picked up, take short breaks after heavy conversations, and remember that caring for someone doesn't mean carrying their feelings for them. Time alone, sleep and saying no to some requests all help.

about: When someone likes you, it tends to show in small, repeated behaviors: they make time for you, pay attention to what you say, look for reasons to be near you and keep conversations going. No single sign proves anything, because some people are friendly with everyone and others hide their feelings when they're shy, but several signs together are worth noticing.

This quiz was written for cv.cm and works for crushes of any gender. Each answer counts as no sign, a small sign or a clear sign, and the total gives you a rough reading. It can't read anyone's mind: the only way to really know is to ask, kindly and in a way that makes it easy for them to say no.

faq.q: How does the quiz score?
faq.a: Each answer is worth 0 to 3 points depending on how strong a sign of interest it is, so the total runs from 0 to 36. 12 or less means few signs, 13 to 24 means mixed signals and 25 or more means lots of signs.

faq.q: What are the clearest signs someone likes you?
faq.a: They start conversations and suggest meeting up, remember small details you told them, make time for you even when busy, and seem happy when you are around. Behavior that keeps repeating matters more than any one moment.

faq.q: They're shy. Could they like me even with a low score?
faq.a: Yes. Shy people often avoid eye contact or go quiet around someone they like. If you're unsure, spend more relaxed time together, one to one, and see whether they open up.

faq.q: How should I tell my crush I like them?
faq.a: Keep it simple and low pressure: suggest a specific plan for just the two of you, or say you enjoy spending time with them and would like to do it more. Give them room to answer honestly, and respect a no.

social-anxiety.title: Social anxiety test: do I have social anxiety? Free self-check — cv.cm
social-anxiety.description: Free social anxiety test: rate 14 statements about meeting people, speaking up and being watched to get a score from 0 to 56 and what it means. Not a diagnosis. Answers stay in your browser.
social-anxiety.lede: Do parties, phone calls or speaking up in a meeting fill you with dread? Rate 14 statements about everyday social situations to see how much social anxiety is shaping your life, and what can help.
about: Social anxiety is a strong, lasting fear of being watched, judged or embarrassed in front of other people. Most people feel nervous before a speech; social anxiety goes further, so that ordinary situations such as eating in public, making a phone call or meeting new people cause intense worry and are often avoided. When it lasts for months and gets in the way of work, study or friendships, doctors call it social anxiety disorder. It is one of the most common anxiety problems, and it responds well to treatment, especially cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).

The statements here were written for cv.cm around the common signs of social anxiety: fear of attention, worry before and after social events, physical symptoms and avoidance. They are not taken from the SPIN, the LSAS or any other questionnaire, and they haven't been clinically validated, so the score bands are a rough guide rather than clinical cut-offs. Half the statements are reversed, so agreeing with everything lands in the middle. Only a doctor or psychologist can diagnose social anxiety disorder.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4 and half are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 56. 18 or less is low, 19 to 37 is moderate and 38 or more is high.

faq.q: What is the difference between shyness and social anxiety?
faq.a: Shyness is a personality trait: you may take a while to warm up, but it doesn't stop you doing things. Social anxiety brings intense fear and worry that lasts before, during and after social situations, and often leads you to avoid them altogether.

faq.q: What are the physical signs of social anxiety?
faq.a: Blushing, sweating, trembling, a racing heart, a shaky voice, feeling sick or your mind going blank when people look at you or you have to speak.

faq.q: Can social anxiety be treated?
faq.a: Yes. Cognitive behavioral therapy, which gradually helps you face feared situations and question anxious thoughts, works well for many people, and some people are also helped by medication. A doctor can talk you through the options.

low.name: Low social anxiety (0–18)
low.body: Social situations don't seem to worry you much. You may still feel nervous before a big presentation or a first date, which is normal. Your ease with people is a strength, and it can help you notice and include friends who find it harder.

moderate.name: Moderate social anxiety (19–37)
moderate.body: Some social situations make you anxious, and you may avoid a few of them. That is common. Small, regular steps help: say yes to one invitation, speak up once in a meeting, and notice that the outcome is usually better than you feared. If the worry is growing or holding you back, talk to a doctor or counselor.

high.name: High social anxiety (38–56)
high.body: Fear of being judged seems to shape a lot of your life, from what you say to where you go. You are not alone, and this is very treatable. Please talk to a doctor or psychologist about it; cognitive behavioral therapy helps many people. If worry follows you outside social situations too, try the GAD-7 anxiety check on this site.

ocd.title: OCD test: do I have OCD? Free obsessive-compulsive self-check — cv.cm
ocd.description: Free OCD test: rate 15 statements about unwanted thoughts, checking, cleaning and rituals over the past month to see whether it's worth asking for an assessment. Not a diagnosis. Answers stay in your browser.
ocd.hint: Thinking about the past month, how well does each statement describe you?
ocd.scoreLabel: OCD self-check score (0 = few signs, 60 = many)
ocd.lede: Do unwanted thoughts keep coming back, or do you feel you have to check, clean or repeat things until they feel right? Rate 15 statements about the past month to help you decide whether to talk to someone about OCD.
about: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) has two parts. Obsessions are unwanted, upsetting thoughts, images or urges that keep pushing into your mind, such as fear of germs, of causing harm or of something being not quite right. Compulsions are things you feel driven to do, out loud or in your head, to ease the anxiety: washing, checking, arranging, counting or seeking reassurance. Many people double-check a lock now and then; in OCD the thoughts and rituals take up a lot of time, cause real distress and get in the way of daily life. About 1 to 3 people in 100 have OCD at some point, and treatment works.

The statements here were written for cv.cm around the main symptom areas of OCD: contamination, checking and doubt, order and symmetry, unwanted thoughts, mental rituals, and the time and distress they take. They are not the Y-BOCS, the OCI-R or any other questionnaire, and they haven't been clinically validated, so the score bands are a rough guide, not clinical cut-offs. Only a doctor or psychologist can diagnose OCD.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree), so the total runs from 0 to 60. 24 or less is few signs, 25 to 39 is some signs, and 40 or more is many.

faq.q: I have disturbing thoughts. Does that mean I will act on them?
faq.a: No. Almost everyone has strange or upsetting thoughts sometimes. In OCD, such thoughts feel so wrong to the person that they cause great distress, which is the opposite of wanting to act on them. A professional can help you deal with them.

faq.q: Is being very tidy or a perfectionist the same as OCD?
faq.a: No. Liking things neat or done well is a personality trait and usually feels good. OCD is driven by anxiety: the rituals feel necessary rather than enjoyable, and they take time and cause distress.

faq.q: How is OCD treated?
faq.a: The main treatment is a type of cognitive behavioral therapy called exposure and response prevention (ERP), which helps you face the fears step by step without doing the ritual. Some people are also helped by medication. A doctor can refer you.

I have avoided touching things like door handles, money or other people's belongings for fear of germs or dirt.
I have gone back, sometimes several times, to make sure a door was locked, an appliance was off or a message was right.
Even after checking something, I have still felt unsure and needed to check again.
I have felt very uncomfortable until things were lined up, even or done in exactly the right order.
I have had to repeat an action, such as flicking a switch or rereading a line, until it felt "just right".
Upsetting thoughts or images have popped into my head that I didn't want and that felt unlike me.
I have worried that just having a bad thought could make something bad happen.
The harder I have tried not to think about something upsetting, the more it has come back.
I have counted, prayed or repeated words in my head to cancel out a bad thought or feeling.
I have asked other people for reassurance again and again about the same worry.
Thoughts or rituals like these have taken up more than an hour on some days.
I have felt anxious or distressed when I couldn't finish a ritual or routine.
I have avoided places, people or tasks because they set off these thoughts or urges.
These thoughts or habits have got in the way of my work, study, sleep or relationships.

few.name: Few signs (0–24)
few.body: You don't report many signs of OCD this past month. Everyone has the odd repeated check or unwanted thought, and that's normal. If something on this list does trouble you, it is still fine to talk to a doctor about it.

some.name: Some signs (25–39)
some.body: You recognize some of these experiences. They may come and go, often getting worse under stress. Notice how much time they take and how distressing they feel. If they are growing or getting in the way of your life, talk to a doctor or psychologist; help works best early.

many.name: Many signs (40–60)
many.body: You recognize many of these experiences, and they seem to take time and cause distress. This doesn't mean you have OCD, but it is a good reason to talk to a doctor or psychologist soon. OCD is very treatable, especially with exposure and response prevention therapy. You don't have to manage it alone.
